questions.question: In a ViewModel, what happens when `api.load()` throws an `IOException`?
options: The catch block never runs: the exception is thrown later inside the coroutine, so the app crashes
The catch block runs and the state becomes `UiState.Error`
The exception is silently swallowed, because `viewModelScope` uses a `SupervisorJob` for its children
It doesn't compile, because try/catch isn't allowed around a coroutine builder
questions.explanation: `launch` only starts the coroutine and returns a `Job`, so the try block has already finished when `load()` throws. The failure goes through the coroutine's Job instead. With no handler it reaches the thread's uncaught exception handler and the app crashes. The try/catch has to go inside the `launch` block.

questions.question: If code inside `withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { ... }` throws, wrapping the `withContext` call in try/catch catches the exception in the calling coroutine.
questions.explanation: `withContext` is a suspending scope function. It waits for its block and rethrows any failure to its caller, the same way `coroutineScope` does. Unlike `launch`, a try/catch around it works.

questions.question: `viewModelScope` is built on a `SupervisorJob`. Why does an uncaught exception in `viewModelScope.launch { }` still crash the app?
options: Supervision only protects the scope; the unhandled exception still reaches the thread's uncaught handler
`viewModelScope` deliberately rethrows every exception on the main thread from `onCleared()`
`SupervisorJob` turns every child exception into a `CancellationException`, which the main looper rethrows
It doesn't crash: exceptions in `viewModelScope` are only logged to Logcat
questions.explanation: Supervision controls whether a failure spreads to the parent and siblings, not whether it gets reported. A coroutine that fails directly under a supervisor has to handle the exception itself, using the `CoroutineExceptionHandler` in its context. Without one, the exception goes to `Thread.uncaughtExceptionHandler`, which on Android crashes the app.

questions.question: A `CoroutineExceptionHandler` can recover from an exception so the failed coroutine continues from the point where it threw.
questions.explanation: When the handler runs, the coroutine has already completed with the exception. The handler is a last resort for logging, reporting or showing an error. To recover and carry on, use try/catch inside the coroutine.

questions.question: `api.sync()` may throw. Which of these stop the exception from crashing the app? Select all that apply.
options: Wrap `api.sync()` in try/catch inside the `launch` block
Wrap the whole `viewModelScope.launch { }` call in try/catch
Move `api.sync()` into a nested `launch(handler) { }` inside the outer `launch`, and put the handler there
questions.explanation: A try/catch inside the coroutine handles the error where it happens. The outer `launch` is a direct child of `viewModelScope`'s `SupervisorJob`, so a handler passed to it is used. A try/catch around `launch` finishes before the coroutine fails. A handler on a nested child is ignored, because the child passes the exception up to its parent.

questions.question: `scope` is `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + handler)` and its `launch` throws `IllegalStateException`. What happens at `job.join()`, called from an unrelated coroutine?
options: `join()` returns normally and `false` is printed, since the job failed rather than being cancelled
`join()` throws a `CancellationException` that wraps the original exception
questions.explanation: `join()` only waits for completion. It never rethrows the job's failure, unlike `await()`. A job that failed with an exception counts as cancelled, so `isCancelled` is `true`.

questions.question: Which statements about exceptions in `async` are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Inside `supervisorScope`, a failing `async` stores the exception in its `Deferred`, and it is thrown only when you call `await()`
As a child of a regular `Job`, a failing `async` cancels its parent even if `await()` is never called
Calling `await()` on a failed `Deferred` rethrows the exception that failed it
Wrapping the `async { }` call itself (not `await()`) in try/catch catches the exception
Calling `await()` a second time on the same failed `Deferred` returns `null` instead of throwing
questions.explanation: `async` stores its result or failure in the `Deferred`, and every `await()` rethrows the failure, not just the first. Under a regular `Job`, a failed child still cancels its parent straight away, so awaiting it is not what triggers that. The `async` call returns immediately, so a try/catch around it catches nothing.

questions.question: The inner child throws. Which handler logs the exception?
options: Neither: the exception goes straight to the thread's uncaught exception handler
questions.explanation: A child of a regular Job doesn't handle its own exception. It passes it up to its parent until it reaches the root coroutine. The root `launch` gets `rootHandler` from the scope and handles the exception, so the handler on the nested child is never used.

questions.question: What does this print?

questions.question: `scope` is `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob())`. `scope.async(handler) { throw RuntimeException() }` runs, and nobody ever calls `await()`. What happens?
options: Nothing is reported: the exception stays in the `Deferred`
The exception goes to the thread's uncaught exception handler and crashes the process
`scope` is cancelled, and all its other coroutines are cancelled with it
questions.explanation: A root `async` expects its caller to handle the exception through `await()`, so a `CoroutineExceptionHandler` has no effect on it. Under a `SupervisorJob` the failure doesn't cancel the scope either. If nobody awaits, the exception is silently lost.

questions.question: If the body of `supervisorScope { }` throws (not a child coroutine), the scope cancels its children and rethrows the exception to the caller.
questions.explanation: Supervision only protects the scope from failures in its children. If the scope's own body throws, the scope fails like any other: it cancels its running children and rethrows, so a try/catch around `supervisorScope` catches it.

questions.question: Which statements about `CancellationException` in coroutines are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A child that throws `CancellationException` does not cancel its parent
Under a regular `Job`, when a child fails with a regular exception, its running siblings get cancelled with a `CancellationException`
An uncaught `CancellationException` is passed to the thread's uncaught exception handler
A child that throws `CancellationException` inside `coroutineScope` makes `coroutineScope` rethrow it as a failure
A child that throws `CancellationException` cancels all of its siblings
questions.explanation: `CancellationException` means "this coroutine was cancelled", so it is not treated as a failure. It isn't reported to any handler, doesn't spread to the parent, and doesn't affect siblings. A regular failure does cancel the parent, and the parent then cancels the remaining children with a `CancellationException`.

questions.question: This runs on the JVM, with no `CoroutineExceptionHandler` anywhere. Child A throws `IOException`. What happens?
options: It goes to the thread's uncaught exception handler, B prints `B done`, and `caught` is never printed
`supervisorScope` waits for B, then rethrows the `IOException`, so `B done` and then `caught` are printed
B is cancelled, and `caught` is printed
The exception is silently dropped and only `B done` is printed
questions.explanation: `supervisorScope` never rethrows a child's failure. It doesn't treat the failure as its own, so the caller's try/catch sees nothing. Each failed child has to handle its own exception, and with no handler that means the thread's uncaught exception handler. On Android, that crashes the app.

questions.question: What's the main coroutine problem with this repository code?

The caller then gets `null` and keeps going as if nothing happened. Rethrow it with `onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }`. `runCatching` is inline, so suspend calls inside it are allowed.
